rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/claim-preserving-writing.md
rows.old_rule_text: Inspect draft, outline, notes, source material, prior posts, templates, house style, venue instructions, and supplied examples before drafting.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Inspect available writing context before drafting or revising.

rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/claim-preserving-writing.md
rows.old_rule_text: Preserve the claim ledger; keep caveats visible; flag unsupported claims.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Separate claims, evidence, assumptions, caveats, and gaps.

rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/language-style-rules.md
rows.old_rule_text: Use short, precise sentences. Replace vague phrases, unexplained metaphors, and overloaded local names.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use short precise sentences and common terminology.

rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/language-style-rules.md
rows.old_rule_text: Define every concept before its first use.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Define non-common concepts before first use.

rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/language-style-rules.md
rows.old_rule_text: Prefer inline equations unless display equations are important.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Prefer inline equations unless display is needed.

rows.source_location: plan_v10
rows.old_rule_text: Finalizable writing workflows must record style_profile_ref and style_applied.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Record active style profile for finalizable writing.

rows.source_location: plan_v10
rows.old_rule_text: Capture new durable user writing requirements and do not promote them without approval.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Capture new durable user style requirements without silent promotion.

rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/language-style-rules.md
rows.old_rule_text: Put concepts and notation used several times in preliminaries; define one-use concepts locally.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Define mathematical concepts and notation before first use.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Never mix statements and definitions. Do not define anything inside a statement.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not define notation inside mathematical statements.

rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/language-style-rules.md
rows.old_rule_text: Prefer standard graph-theoretic and TCS terminology over private vocabulary.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use common graph-theoretic and TCS terminology.

rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/language-style-rules.md
rows.old_rule_text: Restate hypotheses in major results when doing so makes the result self-contained.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep mathematical statements self-contained.

rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/language-style-rules.md
rows.old_rule_text: Add one to three sentences before the statement explaining what the result says and why it is needed.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Introduce important statements with their role.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Each section except Introduction and Concluding remarks should contain a short outline paragraph.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Begin sections with outline paragraphs.

rows.source_location: canonical/instructions/language-style-rules.md
rows.old_rule_text: Start every long or technical proof with a short paragraph giving the proof idea.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Open long proofs with proof ideas.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: For equations, except those which are important, prefer inline equations.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Prefer inline equations unless display is needed.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Never begin a sentence with a verb. Use full sentences always. Prefer short, clear sentences rather than long complicated ambiguous ones. Let ... be ..., Suppose ..., Assume ..., and Recall ... are acceptable.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use full research-paper sentences and avoid command-style openings, while keeping standard mathematical setup and reminder openings when they are clearest.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 11
rows.old_rule_text: All variables must be defined, at least informally, when they are first introduced.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Define each variable, at least informally, where it first appears.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 11
rows.old_rule_text: Try to state things twice, in complementary ways, especially when giving a definition.
rows.normalized_rule_text: State an important definition twice, in complementary ways.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 14
rows.old_rule_text: Don't use the same notation for two different things. Conversely, use consistent notation for the same thing.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use one notation for one thing, and one thing for one notation.

rows.source_location: Tao, Use good notation
rows.old_rule_text: Notation should emphasize the most important parameters and features of a mathematical expression or statement, while downplaying the routine or uninteresting parameters.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Notation should carry the parameters that matter and hide the ones that do not.

rows.source_location: Tao, Use good notation
rows.old_rule_text: Introduce notation for expressions used three or more times; expressions appearing only once typically do not need special notation.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Introduce notation only for what recurs.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 15
rows.old_rule_text: Don't get carried away by subscripts, especially when dealing with a set that doesn't need to be indexed.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not name the elements of a set unless the argument needs them named.

rows.source_location: Tao, Use good notation
rows.old_rule_text: Use bland names for technical or peripheral terms; reserve colorful names for central concepts. Do not name concepts after yourself, family members, or pets.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Give peripheral objects bland names, and do not name a concept after yourself.

rows.source_location: Tao, Use good notation
rows.old_rule_text: Make notation choices compatible with existing literature to help readers familiar with prior work.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Stay compatible with the notation already used in the literature the paper builds on.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 1
rows.old_rule_text: Symbols in different formulas must be separated by words.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Separate symbols belonging to different formulas with words.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 2; West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Don't start a sentence with a symbol.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Never begin a sentence with a symbol.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 3
rows.old_rule_text: Don't use the symbols for all, exists, implies, iff in running text; replace them by the corresponding words.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write logical connectives and quantifiers as words in running prose.

rows.source_location: Tao, Take advantage of the English language
rows.old_rule_text: Humble English words such as 'also', 'but', 'since' indicate how a statement fits in with the rest of one's argument.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep the connective words that tell the reader how each step relates to the last.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 13
rows.old_rule_text: Your sentences should flow smoothly when all but the simplest formulas are replaced by 'blah'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: A sentence should still read smoothly when its formulas are replaced by a nonsense word.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 10
rows.old_rule_text: Don't use the style of homework papers, in which a sequence of formulas is merely listed. Tie the concepts together with a running commentary.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not list formulas without commentary; say what each step does and why.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 26
rows.old_rule_text: Don't use jargon unnecessarily. Even specialists in a field get more pleasure from papers that use a nonspecialist's vocabulary.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not use jargon that the argument does not need.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 26
rows.old_rule_text: Resist the temptation to use long strings of nouns as adjectives.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Avoid long strings of nouns used as adjectives.

rows.source_location: Halmos, in Knuth et al., Mathematical Writing (1989), section 42
rows.old_rule_text: 'Imply' does not mean 'infer', and 'disinterested' does not mean 'uninterested'. To confuse these words is to lose valuable distinctions.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Preserve distinctions the language still makes, such as imply and infer.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), rule 4
rows.old_rule_text: The statement just preceding a theorem, algorithm, etc., should be a complete sentence or should end with a colon.
rows.normalized_rule_text: The sentence immediately before a statement must be complete, or end with a colon.

rows.source_location: Tsitsiklis, Tips on writing papers with mathematical content (2019)
rows.old_rule_text: Short and crisp lemmas, theorems: do not define terms or add discussion inside the statement.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not define terms or add discussion inside a theorem or lemma statement.

rows.source_location: Tsitsiklis, Tips on writing papers with mathematical content (2019)
rows.old_rule_text: We discover proofs by going backwards; we write proofs by going forward, linearly. Outline this structure before starting the proof.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write proofs forwards, and let each sentence rest on what precedes it.

rows.source_location: Halmos, in Knuth et al., Mathematical Writing (1989), section 42
rows.old_rule_text: Proofs by contradiction should not be used if a direct proof is available.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Prefer a direct proof to a proof by contradiction when both are available.

rows.source_location: Tsitsiklis, Tips on writing papers with mathematical content (2019)
rows.old_rule_text: Alert the reader when skipping steps.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Tell the reader when a step is being skipped.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Do not nest proof environments. No new proof label should occur before the end-of-proof marker for the current proof.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not nest proof environments.

rows.source_location: Tsitsiklis, Tips on writing papers with mathematical content (2019)
rows.old_rule_text: Quantifier ambiguities are common: 'for every n, we have n < c, for some c' has two readings.
rows.normalized_rule_text: State quantifiers in an order that admits one reading.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: The word 'any' can mean 'some' or 'all' in different contexts, so it can be imprecise.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use 'each' or 'every' for universal quantification, not 'any'.

rows.source_location: Tsitsiklis, Tips on writing papers with mathematical content (2019); Knuth et al., rule 6
rows.old_rule_text: Active voice: 'We show' vs 'It is shown'. Pronouns must be unambiguous pointers.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Prefer the active voice, and make every pronoun point at exactly one thing.

rows.source_location: Halmos, in Knuth et al., Mathematical Writing (1989), section 42
rows.old_rule_text: Two uses of the same word in unrelated passages will be associated in the reader's mind and cause unwarranted connections.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not echo an unusual word in an unrelated passage.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use 'maximal' for set/object comparisons; use 'maximum' for numerical comparisons. A maximal independent set differs from a maximum independent set.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use maximal and minimal for containment, maximum and minimum for size.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Write 'v in V(G)' and 'e in E(G)' not 'v in G'; graphs are not sets because v could be an edge.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write membership against V(G) or E(G), never against the graph itself.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: 'Order' and 'size' refer to vertex and edge counts respectively.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use order for the vertex count and size for the edge count, or name them explicitly.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: One cannot compare a set to an integer.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Compare cardinalities, not sets, with numbers.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: A clique is a set of pairwise adjacent vertices; a complete subgraph is a subgraph isomorphic to a complete graph.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep clique and complete subgraph distinct.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Do not use 'partition' to refer to members of a partition. Use 'parts' for the members.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use parts for the members of a partition.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Never use Delta to denote the value of Delta(G). Delta is a function, not a number.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write the operator applied to its argument, or bind the value to a name once.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Any operator whose notation is more than one character should be in a different font, generally roman.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Set operators whose names run to more than one character in roman type.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing; Tsitsiklis (2019)
rows.old_rule_text: The expression 'f(n) = O(n^2)' is incorrect; it should be 'f(n) in O(n^2)' or informally 'f(n) is O(n^2)'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Treat Big-Oh as a set, and say what its hidden constant may depend on.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Never write 'a P_n'; write 'a path with n vertices' or 'a copy of P_n'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not use an isomorphism-class symbol as though it named one graph.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Do not say 'directed edge' or 'hyperedges'; these terms eliminate the possibility of stating that these are special cases.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not rename edges in digraphs and hypergraphs.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Say 'components' since all components are connected by definition.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Say components, since every component is connected by definition.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Do not say 'vertex-disjoint'; just say 'disjoint'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Say disjoint unless an edge analogue makes the contrast real.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use 'pairwise' to mean 'for all pairs'; avoid 'mutually' which has different connotations in modern mathematics.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use pairwise for a property holding of all pairs.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use adjectival forms when available: 'Hamiltonian cycle' not 'Hamilton cycle'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use the adjectival form of a personal name, keeping established exceptions.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: A sequence is a function on natural numbers; use 'list' for ordered finite sets. Replace 'degree sequence' with 'degree list'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Prefer degree list where order carries no meaning.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Write 'x,y-path' not 'x-y path' (the latter treats 'x-y' as a meaningless expression).
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write xy-path rather than x-y path. House style departs from the cited source, which writes x,y-path; both avoid the hyphen between the two vertex names.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use 'G-e' not 'G \setminus e' for element deletion; '\setminus' is best reserved for set difference.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Reserve set-minus for set difference and use minus for deletion.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: An edge 'between' u and v should be 'joining u and v' since 'between' typically means separating objects.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Say that an edge joins its ends.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Write 'k-connected graphs' for graphs having k-connectivity; 'k connected graphs' for k separate connected graphs.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Hyphenate a parameter to the property it qualifies.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use '(k+1)-connected graph' with parentheses.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Bracket a compound parameter before its hyphen.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use 'edge-connectivity' and 'edge-chromatic number' with hyphens for edge analogs.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Hyphenate the edge analogue of a vertex parameter.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Hyphenate when placed before the noun: 'polynomial-time algorithm' not 'polynomial time algorithm'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Hyphenate a two-word adjective placed before its noun, and not after it.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Adverbs can modify adjectives without hyphens ('strongly connected'). For 'well-known', hyphenate as a technical term.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not hyphenate an adverb to the adjective it modifies.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing; Knuth et al., rule 21
rows.old_rule_text: Common negations like 'nonsingular', 'nontrivial', 'nonzero' drop the hyphen; less familiar words like 'non-edge' keep it.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Drop the hyphen from familiar negations and keep it on unfamiliar ones.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use colon ':' rather than vertical bar '|' in set definitions because '|' is heavily overused in mathematics.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use a colon rather than a bar in set-builder notation.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Avoid ':='; it encourages grammatical errors.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Avoid colon-equals, which encourages defining and asserting at once.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Write 'v_1,...,v_n' not 'v_1,v_2,...,v_n' since the default interpretation is consecutive indices.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write an indexed list as its first and last terms.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Write 'for m in {1,...,n}' or 'for 1<=m<=n' not 'for m=1,...,n' (mathematically incorrect).
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write a range as membership or as an inequality, not as an equality with a list.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Avoid defining notation and making statements about it simultaneously.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Introduce notation in an appositive, then state facts about it separately.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use 'where' when notation is being defined; use 'such that' when restricting already-defined notation.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use where to introduce notation and such that to restrict it.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use 'such that' when imposing a condition on an object; use 'so that' when describing how an action is performed.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use such that for a condition and so that for a manner.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use 'proper k-coloring' when adjacent elements cannot share colors; omitting 'proper' contradicts combinatorics conventions.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Say proper k-coloring when adjacency constrains the colors.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Avoid placing two formulas consecutively separated only by a comma. Use phrases like 'it follows that' or 'we have' between formulas.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Put words between two consecutive formulas.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Treat notational expressions as single objects (that is, nouns), with some exceptions.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Treat a notational expression as a noun within the sentence.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Words cannot be compared with notation via relational symbols.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write the relation in words when one side of it is a word.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Replace 'Let hypothesis. Then conclusion.' with 'If hypothesis, then conclusion.'
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write a hypothesis and its conclusion as a single if-then sentence.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: When readability improves by omitting 'then', start with 'When' or 'For' instead.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Begin with When or For where the then-clause is dropped.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use words rather than parentheses for restrictions: 'For k<=m with k even' instead of 'For k<=m (k even)'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write a restriction in words rather than in parentheses.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Do not write "v's neighbors"; use 'the neighbors of v' instead.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not attach a possessive to a symbol.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Write 'We use induction on n' not 'We induct on n'. When citing the hypothesis, write 'By the induction hypothesis' not 'By induction'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use induction on a parameter, and cite the induction hypothesis by name.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use as a single predicate adjective without 'the': 'This result is best possible'.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write that a result is best possible, without an article.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: Use 'less' for numbers; use 'fewer' for sets of objects.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use fewer for countable objects and less for quantities.

rows.source_location: West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: The numeral indicating an item in the bibliography should appear immediately after the name(s) of the author(s), not after the statement of the result.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Place a bibliography reference immediately after the name it credits.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Luon su dung template https://github.com/hoanganhduc/TeX-Templates/tree/master/A Simple Article Template
rows.normalized_rule_text: Start a new manuscript from the author's article template.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Bo cac file khong can thiet trong template latex
rows.normalized_rule_text: After copying the template, delete the files the manuscript does not use.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Luon su dung \cref
rows.normalized_rule_text: Make every cross-reference with \cref rather than a bare ef.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Luon su dung biblatex
rows.normalized_rule_text: Manage the bibliography with biblatex and the biber backend.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Luon lam dung yeu cau cua journal/conference khi chuan bi ban camera-ready
rows.normalized_rule_text: Follow the venue's camera-ready instructions exactly, even where they contradict this policy.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Luon su dung ky nang tikz-draw de ve hinh va luon su dung tikz cho cac hinh minh hoa neu co the
rows.normalized_rule_text: Draw figures with TikZ whenever possible, and produce them through the tikz-draw skill.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Luon su dung  egin{enumerate}[(1)] hoac tuong tu de liet ke cac phat bieu can chung minh hay cac dieu kien can thiet lap trong mot phat bieu toan hoc, va trong phan chung minh cung nen co cac phan tuong ung de map ro rang phan nao chung minh cai gi
rows.normalized_rule_text: Enumerate the parts of a statement explicitly, and give the proof the same labelled structure.

rows.source_location: AMS Author Handbook (American Mathematical Society), section on abstracts
rows.old_rule_text: AMS Author Handbook: "The abstract should contain no text references to the bibliography unless the bibliographic reference is fully supplied. For example, [3] is meaningless to the reader once the abstract is separated from the article."
rows.normalized_rule_text: In an abstract, supply any cited work in full, with  ullcite or in words; never cite by number or author-year.

rows.source_location: AMS Author Handbook; arXiv metadata guidance (info.arxiv.org/help/prep.html)
rows.old_rule_text: AMS Author Handbook: "Zentralblatt publishes authors' abstracts instead of reviews, so the abstract may also appear there." arXiv: abstracts are distributed as plain text, longer than 1920 characters will not be accepted, and opaque TeX macros must be expanded.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep the abstract free of references to numbered sections, numbered equations, and the bibliography.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, implicit notational conventions
rows.old_rule_text: The letter x conventionally denotes real numbers, z denotes complex numbers, and n denotes natural numbers; epsilon is reserved for small positive quantities.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Follow the field's implicit conventions about which letters denote what.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, implicit notational conventions
rows.old_rule_text: In X < Y the left side represents an unknown to control and the right a known quantity; main terms should appear first and error terms later.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Put the quantity being controlled on the left of an inequality, and order a bound with its main term first.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, organise the paper
rows.old_rule_text: Each time there is a major turning point in the argument one should start a new section; the statement and proof of lemma X should ideally be placed close to where lemma X is actually used.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Start a new section at each turning point, and place a lemma close to where it is used.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, organise the paper
rows.old_rule_text: The more technical components of the paper should be pushed to the back of the paper if possible, in order to ease the learning curve for the reader.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Put the milestones early and the technical machinery late.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, organise the paper
rows.old_rule_text: Results necessary to the main argument but very different in nature from the rest of the paper belong in appendices; peripheral results belong in remarks, footnotes or discussion sections.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Send material different in nature to an appendix, and demote peripheral results to remarks.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, organise the paper
rows.old_rule_text: Papers where the punch line is delayed until the very last page are particularly frustrating to read.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Never save the main point for the last page.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, motivate the paper
rows.old_rule_text: Before presenting your most general result, it can help to first discuss a less technical special case or toy result first.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Give a toy case or special case before the general result.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, motivate the paper
rows.old_rule_text: Informal, heuristic, or motivational reasoning should be clearly indicated as such to distinguish it from formal, rigorous reasoning.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Mark heuristic and motivational reasoning as such, in a remark or footnote.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, on jumps in difficulty
rows.old_rule_text: Focus on those portions of the argument where the strength of the statements increases significantly; such amplifications often contain an essential trick or idea which powers the entire argument.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Give the most care to the steps where the statements suddenly get stronger.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, on compilation errors in mathematical reading
rows.old_rule_text: A single typo or undefined term in the paper can cause one's comprehension of the paper to grind to a complete halt, in much the same way that it would to a computer.
rows.normalized_rule_text: State the dependency between consecutive steps, and leave no undefined term.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, use the introduction to sell the key points
rows.old_rule_text: The key point is not stated prominently enough in the introduction, instead being buried in a footnote.
rows.normalized_rule_text: State the key point prominently in the introduction.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, use the introduction to sell the key points
rows.old_rule_text: Spend time comparing and contrasting the paper to other literature, and show why the results and techniques are new, interesting or surprising given this context; if new difficulties had to be resolved here which were not present in previous work, these must be prominent.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Compare the work against the literature and name the new difficulties it resolved.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, use the introduction to sell the key points
rows.old_rule_text: Clearly state (or at least paraphrase) the main results of the paper, and outline how and where these results are to be proved; if the main results are too technical, a simpler but still interesting special case can be stated instead.
rows.normalized_rule_text: State or paraphrase the main results and say where each is proved.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, use the introduction to sell the key points
rows.old_rule_text: Present counterexamples showing the result or proof cannot be improved in various obvious directions.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Give counterexamples showing the result cannot be improved in the obvious directions.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, describe the results accurately
rows.old_rule_text: Use informative section titles such as Proof of the decomposition lemma rather than uninformative labels such as Step 2.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Title section headings by their content, not by their position.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, describe the results accurately
rows.old_rule_text: A paper should neither understate nor overstate its main results.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Neither understate nor overstate what was proved.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, describe the results accurately
rows.old_rule_text: State unsatisfactory aspects openly, such as hypotheses too strong or conclusions a little weaker than expected, using formulations like We do not know if hypothesis H is actually necessary.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Say plainly where the result is unsatisfactory, and what is not known.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, describe the results accurately
rows.old_rule_text: It is worth noting down any interesting open questions remaining after your result.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Record the interesting questions left open.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, describe the results accurately
rows.old_rule_text: When asserting non-trivial statements without proof or citation, make this explicit using phrases such as It can be shown that or Although we will not need or prove this fact here.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Mark any non-trivial assertion made without proof or citation.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, describe the results accurately
rows.old_rule_text: Provide candid evaluation of the extent to which your work truly represents progress towards famous conjectures used for motivation, preventing misleading name-dropping.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Say candidly how far the work goes towards any conjecture used as motivation.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, give appropriate amounts of detail
rows.old_rule_text: A paper should dwell at length (using plenty of English) on the most important, innovative, and crucial components.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Dwell on what is important, innovative and load-bearing.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, give appropriate amounts of detail
rows.old_rule_text: Focus on what interests field experts, not personal interests; mastering a standard technique does not justify including its standard proof.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Omit what is routine to an expert in the field.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, give appropriate amounts of detail
rows.old_rule_text: For obscure lemmas from prior work it is worth stating the lemma in full, with a precise citation, and sometimes also worth spending a paragraph to sketch out a proof.
rows.normalized_rule_text: State an obscure lemma from earlier work in full, with a precise citation.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, give appropriate amounts of detail
rows.old_rule_text: Provide readers a clearly circumscribed little problem to solve if they wish to verify details; two trivialities omitted can add up to an impasse.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Whatever is omitted must leave a clearly circumscribed small problem.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, create lemmas
rows.old_rule_text: When facts A, B, C are used only to derive D, encapsulate D as a lemma with A, B, C hidden in its proof.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Encapsulate as a lemma any intermediate fact the main argument would otherwise carry.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, create lemmas
rows.old_rule_text: One should write the statement of a lemma in a way that makes it easy to use, rather than easy to prove.
rows.normalized_rule_text: State a lemma so that it is easy to use, pushing the awkwardness into its proof.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, create lemmas
rows.old_rule_text: Lemmas should explicitly state all the running hypotheses, assumptions, and notational conventions already introduced.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Restate the running hypotheses and conventions inside the lemma.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, create lemmas
rows.old_rule_text: If two technical lemmas are only useful when combined, unify them; the intermediate technical statement becomes a hidden sublemma in the proof.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Merge two lemmas that are only ever useful together.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, do not over-optimise
rows.old_rule_text: A paper which has been overcompressed may be viewed by readers as being more difficult to read.
rows.normalized_rule_text: A shorter paper is not automatically a simpler one.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, do not over-optimise
rows.old_rule_text: Optimising the readability of the paper is always a good thing (except when it is at the expense of rigour or accuracy); carefully optimising results and notations in the hope that this will help future researchers is a little risky.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Optimise readability always; optimise constants and generality only when something depends on it.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, do not over-optimise
rows.old_rule_text: Making hypotheses weaker and conclusions stronger can lengthen proofs and obscure how results connect to the broader paper; state one formulation and add remarks about alternatives.
rows.normalized_rule_text: State one formulation and note the alternative in a remark.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, maximising the results-to-effort ratio
rows.old_rule_text: Any cheap consequences, generalisations, variants, illustrative counterexamples of one's main results should be put into the paper if this can be done with only moderate effort; if a huge fraction of the paper is devoted to only a minor extension, one may consider removing that section.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Include cheap consequences; cut a section whose length is out of proportion to what it adds.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, write in your own voice
rows.old_rule_text: It is best to paraphrase and interpret the previous text rather than to copy that text verbatim; if one is paraphrasing a previous work, one should cite that work appropriately.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Paraphrase and cite earlier work; do not copy its text.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, write in your own voice
rows.old_rule_text: Direct quotations should illustrate historical points only; excessive quotation reads as name-dropping.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Reserve direct quotation for a historical point.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, write in your own voice
rows.old_rule_text: Writing that mixes multiple authors' voices can read very strangely, and mimicking senior mathematicians' styles is often found offensive.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write in your own voice rather than imitating a particular author.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, write professionally
rows.old_rule_text: References should be current, showing all recent related work, with accurate assignment of credit, provenance, and precedence; keep personal opinions clearly labelled and separate from objective assertions.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Assign credit and precedence accurately, and mark a judgement as a judgement.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, write professionally
rows.old_rule_text: Overly philosophical, witty, obscure or otherwise clever comments should generally be avoided.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Avoid witty, philosophical or knowingly obscure asides.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, submit a final draft, not a first draft
rows.old_rule_text: It is not yet time to submit the paper to a journal if you are still finding typographical or other errors, or still adding results and commentary.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not submit while still finding errors or still adding results.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, proofread and double-check your paper before submission
rows.old_rule_text: Give particular scrutiny to citations; look up primary sources to double check that the citations are being handled properly, and ensure important references are not mentioned only tangentially, cited inaccurately, or omitted altogether.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Check every citation against the primary source.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, write professionally
rows.old_rule_text: Careless English conveys the impression that the paper itself is also careless.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Treat careless English as a correctness signal, not only a style one.

rows.source_location: Terence Tao, On writing, submit a final draft, not a first draft
rows.old_rule_text: When sharing drafts with colleagues, send a version of the paper that already has been proofread and to which a significant amount of work has already gone into improving the exposition.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Send colleagues a proofread draft, not an early one.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Nen su dung latex voi cac ky hieu toan hoc trong cac huong dan. Vi du khong nen viet xy-path ma nen viet $xy$-path.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Write notation as LaTeX in math mode, in these policy documents and in the manuscript, including bare variable names.

rows.source_location: user-requirement; departs from West, Grammar and technical writing
rows.old_rule_text: West: Hence and Thus may be used without commas (as single syllables indicating argument flow), while Therefore takes a comma for major conclusions.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Put a comma after every introductory word or phrase, including the monosyllables Hence and Thus. House style is uniform where the cited source allows an exception.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Khi su dung mot khai niem la, can truoc tien tim hieu xem co khai niem nao tuong tu da duoc dinh nghia truoc do chua, va neu co thi nen dung khai niem da dinh nghia truoc do neu co the thay vi ve voi ra them dinh nghia.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Before defining a new concept, search for an existing one that covers it, and use the established name and notation when one exists.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Neu phai dat khai niem moi thi phai noi ro no tong quat hoa hay dac biet hoa cai gi, va vi sao khai niem san co khong du.
rows.normalized_rule_text: When coining a concept, name the closest existing notion and say why it does not suffice.

rows.source_location: user-requirement
rows.old_rule_text: Het suc tranh su dung cac tu ngu va van phong la lam, lam kho nguoi doc. Luon su dung cac tu don gian va thuong gap va de hieu hon.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Choose the simpler and more common word where one exists, and keep sentence forms ordinary.

rows.source_location: user-requirement; West, Grammar and technical writing (italics for defined words)
rows.old_rule_text: Words being defined should be distinguished by italics (or perhaps boldface in a textbook context). User requirement: khi dinh nghia mot thuat ngu lan dau tien trong bai viet, luon su dung \emph{}.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Mark a term with \emph at the point where it is defined, and only there; prefer \emph to 	extit because emphasis nests inside italic contexts.

rows.source_location: Trzeciak, Writing Mathematical Papers in English (rev. ed., 2005), pp. 16, 29-30, 47; Strunk and White, The Elements of Style, 4th-edition text, rule I.11; Krantz, A Primer of Mathematical Writing (2nd ed., 2017), section 1.4
rows.old_rule_text: An opening participial phrase must refer to the grammatical subject that performs its action.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Attach an opening participial phrase to the grammatical subject it modifies, or replace it with an explicit clause.

rows.source_location: Trzeciak, Writing Mathematical Papers in English (rev. ed., 2005), pp. 44-45; Strunk and White, The Elements of Style, rule I.3; Krantz, A Primer of Mathematical Writing (2nd ed., 2017), section 1.11
rows.old_rule_text: Restrictive and nonrestrictive clauses require different comma treatment, and mathematical scope must remain unambiguous.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Punctuate restrictive and nonrestrictive clauses by meaning and insert commas where omission would obscure scope.

rows.source_location: Trzeciak, Writing Mathematical Papers in English (rev. ed., 2005), pp. 23, 46; Merriam-Webster, A vs. An: When to Use Indefinite Articles, accessed 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: The choice between a and an follows pronunciation, including before symbols and abbreviations.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Choose a or an by the sound that follows rather than by the first written letter.

rows.source_location: user requirement; clause audit of the retired language-style compatibility source
rows.old_rule_text: Use theorem, proposition, lemma, and corollary environments instead of a generic Statement environment.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use the mathematical statement environment that names the result's role.

rows.source_location: Holst, Scientific Paper Writing (2015), section 5.3, pp. 69-79; Krantz, A Primer of Mathematical Writing (2nd ed., 2017), section 2.5, pp. 68-69
rows.old_rule_text: An abstract should state the problem or context, main result, novelty, and only the method needed to understand the contribution.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Give a mathematical abstract its essential context, result, novelty, limitation, and contribution-bearing method.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), section 37, pp. 91-92
rows.old_rule_text: Running prose should remain readable when headings or parenthetical citations are removed for inspection.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use omission only as a readability test; delivered prose retains required citations and attribution.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), sections 18-21, pp. 37-46
rows.old_rule_text: Use an illustration when prose leaves a structure opaque, keep it near the explanation, and make related examples build on one another.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use and place a figure for semantic clarity without turning the writing rule into figure-generation authority.

rows.source_location: user requirement; general standard-source policy, with Diestel and West retained only as candidate graph-theory references
rows.old_rule_text: Do not omit a graph-theoretic definition as standard without checking a standard source; named textbooks are suggestions rather than fixed authority.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Verify a standard source before omitting a basic graph definition, without canonizing one author or edition.

rows.source_location: retired claim-preserving-writing compatibility document; clause-level audit completed 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: After substantive rewriting, track added, removed, strengthened, weakened, unsupported, caveat-changed, and support-changed claims; remove or explicitly accept unsupported additions.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Audit every semantic revision delta and require support or explicit acceptance before readiness.

rows.source_location: Holst, Scientific Paper Writing (2015), sections 4.2 and 6.1, pp. 47-49, 108-114
rows.old_rule_text: Identify the main claim before drafting and align sections, figures, tables, and evidence with it.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Record the primary claim and map every substantive draft component to the claim it supports.

rows.source_location: Holst, Scientific Paper Writing (2015), section 6.1.1, pp. 115-116, corrected by COPE Text Recycling Guidelines
rows.old_rule_text: Cosmetic alteration does not make reused text or figures original; legitimate reuse depends on transparency, attribution, copyright, license, and venue rules.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Disclose and cite self-reuse and obtain permission when the governing terms require it.

rows.source_location: Holst, Scientific Paper Writing (2015), section 5.12 and related publication tactics, corrected by current ICMJE reference guidance
rows.old_rule_text: References must be selected for relevance and support rather than to influence editors, reviewers, or metrics.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Forbid citation manipulation while preserving relevant self-citation and accurate credit.

rows.source_location: Krantz, A Primer of Mathematical Writing (2nd ed., 2017), sections 1.3.3, 1.6.1, 5.6.4 and 5.7.6-5.7.11; Knuth et al., Mathematical Writing (1989), sections 6-8 and 34-41
rows.old_rule_text: Separate mathematical, structural, prose, notation, and surface-copyediting passes and recheck after production edits.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use multiple review passes and verify that editorial changes preserve mathematics and references.

rows.source_location: Trzeciak, Writing Mathematical Papers in English (rev. ed., 2005), Word Order, pp. 40-43
rows.old_rule_text: Place only and other scope-bearing modifiers next to the expression they modify.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep scope-bearing modifiers adjacent to their targets.

rows.source_location: Holst, Scientific Paper Writing (2015), section 14.2; Krantz, A Primer of Mathematical Writing (2nd ed., 2017), sections 2.7.7-2.7.10 and 5.7.4-5.7.6
rows.old_rule_text: Every reviewer request needs a recorded disposition and any resulting semantic change must remain auditable.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Close review comments through a redacted disposition map without granting reviewers edit authority.

rows.source_location: local safeguard derived from AMS and zbMATH assigned-material restrictions; reviewed 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: Determine service, provenance, artifact, terms, destination, purpose, retention, and deletion conditions before any content-accessing tool call.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Fail closed on unknown or mixed review-material provenance before content access.

rows.source_location: AMS Mathematical Reviews Guide for Reviewers, Content of a review, page states Updated February 2015, https://mathscinet.ams.org/mresubs/guide-reviewers.html, accessed 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: Material supplied by Mathematical Reviews may not be uploaded to LLM or AI tools; grammar checking the review itself is permitted.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Block AI processing of MR-supplied material and narrow the permitted lane to surface checking of isolated reviewer-authored prose.

rows.source_location: zbMATH Guide for Reviewers, updated 2024-11-01, Legal Matters and use restrictions, https://zbmath.org/static/guide-for-reviewers-letter.pdf; relevant text inspected through indexed extraction and official Prague guidance
rows.old_rule_text: Service-provided electronic items are for reviewing only, may not be circulated, and may carry deletion conditions.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep zbMATH-supplied material within its authorized review use without attributing an unverified AI-specific ban.

rows.source_location: local safeguard reviewed 2026-09-13; source-grounded authorization boundary
rows.old_rule_text: A separately obtained public copy is a distinct artifact and does not reclassify a restricted supplied copy.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Require artifact-specific processing permission and separate reading authority from execution authority.

rows.source_location: AMS Mathematical Reviews Guide for Reviewers, page states Updated February 2015, accessed 2026-09-13; zbMATH Guide for Reviewers, updated 2024-11-01; Edward Dunne, MathOverflow answer 2021-01-28
rows.old_rule_text: A bibliographic review helps a reader decide whether to read the item by explaining context, main result, and method or proof idea.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Organize a concise decision-to-read review around context, result, and method at the appropriate technical level.

rows.source_location: zbMATH Guide for Reviewers, updated 2024-11-01, Contents of Reviews
rows.old_rule_text: A zbMATH review must add information rather than copy or minimally vary the abstract; extensive direct quotes must be identified.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Require independent added value beyond the abstract and transparent quotation treatment.

rows.source_location: AMS Mathematical Reviews Guide for Reviewers, page states Updated February 2015, accessed 2026-09-13, fallback treatments
rows.old_rule_text: An insightful independent review is preferred to using the author summary or publishing without a review.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Treat MR fallback treatments as service-specific exceptions rather than drafting shortcuts.

rows.source_location: AMS Mathematical Reviews Guide for Reviewers, page states Updated February 2015, Evaluative reviews; MathOverflow discussions on useful MathSciNet and zbMATH reviews, accessed 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: The factual account is primary; evaluation is optional and should not turn the review into promotion.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Separate evidence-bound evaluation from the mathematical and bibliographic record.

rows.source_location: AMS Mathematical Reviews Guide for Reviewers, page states Updated February 2015, Evaluative reviews; zbMATH Guide for Reviewers, Contents of Reviews
rows.old_rule_text: Criticism, error, and overlap claims must be precise, documented, and supported by locations, counterexamples, or exact references.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Require auditable evidence for negative mathematical assessments.

rows.source_location: zbMATH Guide for Reviewers, updated 2024-11-01, Contents of Reviews
rows.old_rule_text: A zbMATH review is not a referee report and should not recommend prepublication changes to an already published item.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep public bibliographic review separate from prepublication refereeing.

rows.source_location: AMS and zbMATH reviewer guides; MathOverflow How to write a good MathSciNet review, accessed 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: Related work, later developments, alternative terms, search terms, and prerequisites add value only when useful and verified.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Use a few verified connections to improve context and discoverability without reproducing a bibliography.

rows.source_location: AMS Mathematical Reviews Guide for Reviewers, page states Updated February 2015, live page accessed 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: MR reviews follow current English, length, reference, MR-number, MSC, and proof-preview requirements.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Resolve current MR delivery constraints from the official guide before finalizing a review.

rows.source_location: zbMATH Guide for Reviewers, updated 2024-11-01; zbMATH review template v2.1, 2021-06-24
rows.old_rule_text: zbMATH reviews follow current language, MSC, keyword, standard-LaTeX, package, and proofreading requirements.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Resolve current zbMATH delivery constraints from the official guide and template instead of hard-coding a package list.

rows.source_location: AMS Beyond Reviews exceptional-review collection; MathOverflow example discussions; Krantz, A Primer of Mathematical Writing (2nd ed., 2017), sections 4.2-4.3
rows.old_rule_text: Examples can guide selection of context, definitions, prerequisites, results, methods, and book-review features without imposing a voice or rigid outline.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Treat exceptional reviews and book-review advice as heuristics rather than venue rules.

rows.source_location: Holst, Scientific Paper Writing (2015), source audit 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: Optimize authorship, citations, result selection, or reviewer response to influence prestige, metrics, or editorial psychology.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Reject strategic publication tactics that weaken truth, relevance, attribution, or affirmative author approval.

rows.source_location: Strunk and White, The Elements of Style, machine-readable 4th-edition text; source audit 2026-09-13; exact Penguin 2007 attachment unverified
rows.old_rule_text: Apply dated or disputed word bans, pronoun rules, data agreement, which/that rules, or other usage prescriptions as universal policy.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep dated usage prescriptions reference-only and use current grammar evidence for promoted rules.

rows.source_location: Knuth, Larrabee and Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989), source audit 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: Import literate-programming, user-manual, program-presentation, code-naming, or obsolete TeX mechanics into scientific prose policy.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep code-writing and obsolete tooling guidance outside the prose policy.

rows.source_location: Krantz, A Primer of Mathematical Writing (2nd ed., 2017), source audit 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: Promote fixed theorem-length limits, personal bibliography preferences, software brands, file-transfer mechanics, or dated MathSciNet/zbMATH facts.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep numerical, personal, tool-specific, and stale publishing advice non-normative.

rows.source_location: Trzeciak, Writing Mathematical Papers in English (rev. ed., 2005), conflict audit 2026-09-13
rows.old_rule_text: Prefer blanket imperative openings, omit hypotheses needed for self-containment, or make introductory commas optional.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Preserve the user-approved sentence-opening, self-contained-statement, and introductory-comma rules.

rows.source_location: user-directed post-publication review revision, 2026-09-14; synthesis of the current review workflow
rows.old_rule_text: A review should make clear why the intended database reader might consult the item, without turning the opening into promotion.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Require a factual contribution thesis that states what the item adds and its relevance to the intended reader.

rows.source_location: user-directed post-publication review revision, 2026-09-14; synthesis of the current review workflow
rows.old_rule_text: A bibliographic review need not list every theorem and should select results according to their explanatory role.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Select representative results proportionately rather than defaulting to a theorem inventory.

rows.source_location: user-directed post-publication review revision, 2026-09-14; evidence-first synthesis of the current review workflow
rows.old_rule_text: Claims that a contribution is important must explain the verified mathematical or literary basis for that importance.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Ground asserted importance, novelty, or significance in a concrete verified contribution without inflating descriptive claims.

rows.source_location: local safeguard for both post-publication bibliographic-review workflows, reviewed 2026-09-14
rows.old_rule_text: Post-publication bibliographic reviews should inform readers rather than simulate an acceptance report or requested-revision letter.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Keep both public bibliographic-review workflows distinct from prepublication refereeing while permitting verified reader-relevant corrections.

rows.source_location: user correction after exact-context review of a theorem claim, 2026-09-14
rows.old_rule_text: An apparent counterexample is not a refutation when an established contextual assumption rules it out; a newly invented rescue assumption is different.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Check the exact version and all relevant contextual assumptions before classifying a mathematical criticism, and distinguish a proof gap from a false theorem.

rows.source_location: user correction after comparing PDF extraction with the exact arXiv source and publication context, 2026-09-14
rows.old_rule_text: OCR or extracted text can corrupt a theorem statement, and source from another version can use different notation.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Verify wording-sensitive criticism against the exact reviewed version and record notation correspondences across versions.

rows.source_location: user requirement, 2026-09-14
rows.old_rule_text: Each sentence must start on its own source line and may span further lines when needed; no source line may contain prose from multiple complete sentences.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Never place prose from multiple complete sentences on one physical source line in active or commented .tex source; allow a single sentence to span lines and do not constrain rendered PDF layout.

rows.source_location: user requirement and clarification, 2026-09-14
rows.old_rule_text: Commenting out unused content inside a LaTeX file preserves it for later restoration; deleting a whole unnecessary file is a separate operation.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Preserve superseded or unused .tex content in comments by default, delete it when genuinely necessary, require removal across confidentiality, privacy, security, licensing, anonymization, redaction, or unsafe-content boundaries, and keep whole-file deletion outside this rule.

rows.source_location: user correction removing an unapproved local provenance precondition, 2026-09-14
rows.old_rule_text: A request for a Mathematical Reviews/MathSciNet or zbMATH review does not establish that the local or user-provided item was supplied by that service.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Do not require a provenance declaration or block access to ordinary local, user-provided, or public review material unless the user or artifact identifies it as service-supplied.

rows.source_location: user correction removing all unrequested review-material restrictions, 2026-09-14
rows.old_rule_text: Do not add restrictions in review workflows unless the user requested them or a directly verified source requires them.
rows.normalized_rule_text: Prohibit unrequested access, transfer, compilation, delegation, retention, and deletion restrictions in MathSciNet and zbMATH review guidance.
